sections.title: Ask yourself
content: Why do you want to leave the power company? If your answer is to make better money and retirement and further your career as a journeyman lineman. The road could help you obtain these goals. You probably have many questions.  I was once in your shoes. A young man, I just quit the best job I ever had. A job that I invested so much time and effort into. Quit hooked up to a camper and drove 3,000 miles across the country. In hopes that when I got to where I was going, I would be able to get a job and continue making money. Talk about a stressful situation.

sections.title: Get comfortable with being uncomfortable
content: I can confidently say that the IBEW has granted me with work every time I have needed it. Don’t get me wrong, there have been tough times. Work is slow, things in life require you to be close to home. Work might not be close to home. Other times work is close to home; you’re making way better money. The financial stress is off your back. Everything is exactly how it was explained to you. Through the hard times you will grow to understand that it is a part of the process. When the hard times are over and things are great you can reflect on the hard times and understand that everything is going to be fine. Try not to let things make you make irrational decisions.

sections.title: What do I need to leave
content: To start you’ll need to obtain an A membership at the union hall. To put it simply, an A membership will give you the opportunity to travel as a journeyman lineman. It does have other benefits to it that we won’t get into at this point. You’re just trying to leave. Often, you’ll hear the term Golden Ticket. Partly because it is yellow in color and the other part being it will grant you work wherever you would like in the country. That yellow ticket is gold in your pocket.

sections.title: The Golden Ticket
content: All you have to do is go up to the hall and ask to be upgraded to an A member if you’re not already an A member. Then pay a head 3 months of dues. This ensures that you’re up to date on your dues. Then this is where you’ll receive a “dues receipt” the Golden Ticket. This ticket will have a number on it that was assigned to you when you joined the IBEW. That ticket number is very important. You’ll hear what is your ticket number 100 times its good to memorize it. You always want to stay up to date on your dues, this ensures that you’re in good standing with the hall. You must be in good stand with the hall to get Letters of Introduction sent to the other halls you wish to work out of. We will come back to this shortly.

sections.title: OSHA 10 T&D
content: This is going to be a 10-hour OSHA class that’s typically broken down for 2 days. Most union halls will provide this class every so often. LU 222 (FREE for IBEW members) for example will post this on their Facebook or website. Usually held quarterly along with first aid CPR. Sign up and take the course. It is critical because you cannot obtain a job from the hall without an OSHA 10 T&D. In this course you will learn OSHA standards for transmission and distribution. “T&D”. If the nearest hall to you is not offering the course you may have to travel to another hall to take it. The hall will not accept online courses.
checklist: Find the next in-person OSHA 10 T&D class at a union hall
Register and complete the class
Save a photo of the completion card/certificate

sections.title: First Aid/ CPR/ AED
content: If you’re currently working for a company that requires you to have first aid CPR AED, then you can request a copy of the card from the company that provided the training. If the card happens to be out of date you can wait until your next training or you can sign up for a local training course nearer to you. Or the hall will provide classes usually quarterly at the local 222. This course must be taken in person the hall will not accept online courses.
checklist: Confirm your card is current (in-person only)
Request a copy of your current card from your employer or instructor
If expired, schedule an in-person recertification

sections.title: DOT Medical Card
content: Look in your area at the nearest walk-in clinic that offers DOT physicals. You potentially will have to schedule an appointment some, offer walk ins. They will do a basic physical. They’ll check your blood pressure, hearing, eyes just the name a few. It’s not extensive at all. Basically, they’re making sure you’re not going to die soon while driving a CDL vehicle down the road. I will tell the story of my first DOT physical where the nurse went to the corner of a 10’x10’ room and whispered the number 7. Then she asked me what number I heard. Yeah, it’s that serious. This medical card will be good for 2 years after. It will need to be updated every 2 years. If you do have a medical issue, they can deny you a medical card. It rarely happens. They can also issue you a 1-year card with the anticipation that you’ll get the medical issue taken care of.
checklist: Schedule or walk in for a DOT physical
Obtain your DOT medical card (usually valid 2 years)
Set a reminder before it expires

sections.title: Update your CDL
content: Now that you’ve obtained your DOT medical card. You need to take it up to the DMV and update it to your CDL. Doing this you will go from an Intra-State driver to an Inter-State driver. This will allow you to drive a CDL vehicle anywhere not just in the state of which you received your driver’s license. It is critical that you get your driver's license changed to INTER-STATE. Don’t be like me and have no clue and just put down what sounded correct. It will mess things up. You don’t need any more stress.
checklist: Bring DOT medical card to the DMV
Update your CDL status to INTER-STATE
Verify the DMV updated your record correctly

sections.title: Tools/Gear
content: You’re required to have a set of climbing tools. Typically, a basic set of hand tools are needed. Check with the hall, they will have a list of tools you’re required to have. The list may vary. If you want specialty tools, battery tools, and tools outside of the lists you can buy whatever tools you want to use. If you have a set of climbing tools, you’ll also have some sort of fall arrest belt. If you don’t have fall arrest the company must provide you with one. Same with any other PPE items. Hard hat, leather gloves, body harness, rubber gloves, rubber sleeves and glasses.
checklist: Get the hall’s required tool list
Acquire required climbing tools and basic hand tools
Confirm employer provides fall arrest belt/PPE if you don’t have it

sections.title: You did it
content: At this point you have everything you need to leave the power company. To get all the items listed above, it won’t take long. The OHSA 10 would take the longest due to classes being available. Keep in mind that you can obtain all of this while still employed by the power company. I would highly recommend getting everything before resigning from the company. The only case that would make sense is if you’re financially able to not collect a check while obtaining these items. I would recommend everyone to have these items if you’re leaving or not. You never know what could happen. If you get fired for example.

sections.title: Localize All Documents
content: To make it easier on yourself, have pictures of all your documents in an album on your phone. This makes for easier access, and it saves time when signing books and during your on-boarding. Keep all physical documents together and on your person when on-boarding or signing the books in person or E-board meetings. Call the hall to find out what documents you will need for different occasions.
checklist: Create a phone album with photos of all required documents
Keep physical documents together for onboarding and book signing
Call the hall to confirm what each local requires

sections.title: Things to consider
content: You’ll have vacation and sick time to burn; retirement left behind a potential gap in health insurance. Let’s start with sick and vacation time. Depending on the union contract, the vacation and sick time is a bargained agreement. The IBEW fought and voted to have these benefits. They are yours to use as you please. It’s all dependent on the contract. I’ve heard that some companies will “cut you a check” for the remaining vacation. From my experience the company that I left will not pay you for sick time, but they will pay you for vacation or allow you to burn your time. Long story short have a plan on how you will use your time, so you don’t lose it.

sections.title: Roll your retirement
content: Ultimately, you’ll need to decide what you want to do with the retirement you gained while working for the company. I rolled my retirement into a Roth IRA. The Retirement outside is NEAP National Electrical Annuity Plan. This is a pretax annuity plan. From what I gather you can roll other pretax plans into this plan. Once you roll it in it’s very hard to roll it back out. There are only 3 ways I can gather. You retire or separate from IBEW covered employment. You reach 59 and ½ and are eligible under current plan rules. Disability or Death. Your choice. Have a plan, but not something that you have changed at once.
checklist: Decide where your prior retirement funds should roll over
Understand NEAP rules and limitations on roll-outs
Document your plan so you don’t change it impulsively

sections.title: Potential gap in health insurance
content: When initially going to outside construction your health insurance will be with Lineco. You will not automatically get health insurance. To obtain the insurance you must work at least 125 hours per month. So, in basic terms, you won’t have insurance for the first month of working. Once hours are reported, which can take a little longer than a month in some cases. Lineco will then see the hours and start the initiation of your health insurance. Which takes another month. During this time if you must go to the doctor, I was told by lineco to keep receipts and they would reimburse. Whatever month you officially leave the power company will be the month that your insurance runs out. Example, if you leave December 1st, you will be covered until the end of December. You may consider being strategic with burning the time that is due to you from the company. This is not considered double booking. You’re not physically working for the company anymore. You’re burning time that you earned. Example if you have 4 weeks of vacation and 2 weeks of sick you leave the company in January. You burn your time this will get you into the middle of February. Hopefully you picked a job up in the beginning of January after you left the company. You worked 125 hours in January lineco process initiates. You work another 125 hours in February. March 1st you’ll have lineco insurance and you never had a gap in insurance. Because the time you burnt from the company ended your insurance with the company at the end of February.
checklist: Understand LINECO eligibility (125 hours/month)
Plan your resignation date and time-off burn to avoid insurance gaps
Keep receipts if you must pay out of pocket during transition

sections.title: Travel Letter
content: A formal document that must be sent from your current hall to the hall you wish to transfer your ticket to. Basically, saying that you’re in good standing with your hall. Also has your ticket number and address where you live. This can be done by the business agent at your hall or the office manager.
checklist: Ask your current hall to send a travel letter to the destination hall
Confirm it includes ticket number, address, and good standing status

sections.title: Transferring your ticket
content: A critical step that shouldn’t be overlooked for many reasons. Can I travel with my utility local ticket? Yes, you can but let’s go through the reasons why getting it transferred to the outside construction local is important. For starters your dues will be much cheaper. When you pay your dues at the utility local you pay working dues as well as regular dues. At the outside local you’ll only be paying your regular dues to your home local. Your working dues will be a percentage paid out of your check. Those dues are paid to the local you’re working out of. Second, typically the utility local doesn’t take part in ERTS. The Electronic Reciprocal Transfer System (ERTS) — “Enabling the transfer of members’ pension and health & welfare contributions back to their home funds, no matter where they may be working.” I’m going to try to explain this as easily as possible. Certain outside locals don’t take part in the same benefits as other outside locals do. For example, the local 1249 does have lineco for health care and a different retirement plan. Without ERTS transferring your hours back to your home local the hall wouldn’t know that you’re getting hours reported. Thus, you will lose your insurance. I’m speaking from experience. This happened to me. I was 20 hours from home in New York. Trust me, you don’t want the stress. And lastly, if you don’t transfer your ticket to the outside local in the state you live in. You will be a book 2 traveler in your home state. Not cool, I did it. Really sucked seeing calls close to the house with no chance of getting the calls at 200 on book 2.

sections.title: Letter Of Introduction
content: As said above you will need a letter of introduction sent the all the halls that you wish to work out of. This is a simple task. I will email the hall and ask them to send LOIs to whatever hall I’m wanting to work out of. A LOI is a letter saying that you’re in good standing at your home local. Your dues are paid and your hall is introducing you to their hall.
checklist: Request LOIs from your home hall for locals you plan to sign
Confirm each LOI is sent before you sign books

sections.title: The Books
content: Basically, a list of people who are currently out of work. Each hall will have a set of books. We'll focus only on books 1 and 2, though books 3 and 4 exist. Starting with the term book 1 hand. You’re a book 1 hand at your home local. In my case when I transferred my ticket from the utility local 108 to the 222. I am now book 1 at 222. Typically, you live in that state. Not a requirement for some, but most locals it’s a requirement. Book 1 hands are going to get an opportunity at every job before a book 2 hand does. The only way a book 2 hand gets a call Is if the call wasn’t filled by book 1 hands. As you’ve probably gathered a book 2 hand is a traveler. He is out of work and looking to other locals for work.

sections.title: Signing The Books
content: When you’re out of work, that is when you sign the books. You can sign as many books as you want while you’re out of work. As said above, you can only be on book 1 at your home local. When signing books, you will need all the items listed above plus a letter of introduction. Some halls will require you to sign the books in person. Meaning you will have to travel to the hall, walk in and sign. Other halls will allow you to sign the book online. Which can be done via email, phone call, or website. Your best bet is to call the hall and get your questions answered before you sign in person or online. You want to call before dispatch starts dispatching calls. Usually, 9:00am is when dispatch starts. You can sign in the afternoon. Just get familiar with when to call or walk in to sign.
checklist: Gather required docs + LOI for each local
Confirm whether each local requires in-person signing
Learn dispatch hours before you call or show up

sections.title: The Strike System
content: This refers to the process of denying calls. If you’re called with a job from the hall and deny the call, you will receive a strike. Once you receive 3 strikes you will roll to the bottom of the book. That can be book 2 if you’re traveling or book 1 at your home local. As you gain strikes you move higher up the list. This could mean that you’ll have a better chance of getting better calls. Or the opposite you could end up striking out because all the calls don’t meet your requirements. It’s a gamble, but it keeps the book from going stale. Typically, you will get strikes for the same call 2 days in a row depending on the local. You won’t get strikes on calls that you don’t meet the requirements for. Like if you don’t have a crane certificate you won’t get a strike for a call that requires a crane certificate.

sections.title: Re-Sign
content: To keep the books current and to see who is really looking for jobs. There is a re-sign period. This period varies local to local. Most locals I’ve worked out of do a re-sign period between the 10th-16th of every month. They’re not all the same. When signing the books it will be mentioned when the re-sign period is. If you forget to resign you will fall completely off of the book. This can be critical if the local requires you to sign in person. Meaning you would have to travel back to the local and sign the books again. You won’t have to re-sign in person, usually you can re-sign online or through an app. You can also call and re-sign over the phone.
checklist: Learn each local’s monthly re-sign window
Set a monthly reminder to re-sign
Know the re-sign method (phone/app/online/in-person)

sections.title: Where Is The Work
content: This question has many different variables. As I said above, your best bet is to call the hall. To keep it simple if you have no desire to work in a certain state don’t sign their books. There are some online tools that will give you a snapshot into what work looks like. The tools are vague. This is where building a quality network helps. You can call pals you’ve worked with in the past. Catch up with them, see where they’re working, if they’re hearing any rumors of where the works moving. Also, some halls will show their job calls online, some won’t unless you’re signed up on their books. Simply google IBEW local 222 job board as an example. If they have one available, you’ll be able to see the calls.

sections.title: Standing Calls
content: Often referred to as, “open calls”. If a call stands that means the call made it all the way through book 1 and 2 and no one took the call. This could be for many reasons. Bad area, no per diem, not enough hours, or work could be moving so well that calls are just standing due to lack of people on the books. Depending on the hall, this call is available for anyone to take. Always a good idea to become familiar with the rules for standing calls at each local, they all can be different. In my case when signing the 1245 books the 1st time I signed in the afternoon around 2pm. They had already dispatched all the calls that day and there were standing calls when I signed. I took one of the many calls they had available before I walked out the door. “The halls a walkthrough” a saying when work is moving so well that you walk right through with a job. No waiting.

sections.title: Short Calls
content: The time can vary at each local. It’s a good idea to understand the local’s rules on short calls. Basically, the call in the description will say short call. Which means, for example, the call is only for 2 weeks. Could be more could be less depending on the local’s rules. Most locals that I have worked out of have a rule that if you take a short call, once you’re laid off you will call the hall and provide a term slip. Then the hall will put you back on the books in the position you were in when you took the call example book 2 #20 2 strikes. You may take a short call to play the books because you have 2 strikes and you don’t want to roll to the back of the book. Just remember you’ll be back on the book after the short call with the 2 strikes.

sections.title: Referral
content: When you take a call out of the hall, the hall will send you a referral with all the information that was on the call. It will have show up times and addresses to the show up as well as the location where you will on-board. It will have the General Foreman’s contact information. You need to get ahold of the GF ASAP. He will answer any questions you may have. Be sure that the information on the referral is correct. Meaning the hours that the job will be (5-10s) and the per diem. Sometimes per diem will be called sub. Double sub is $100 a day and so forth.

sections.title: Loaded Calls
content: This will be a good segway into “getting spun” in the next section. When looking at calls on the books some calls will be loaded. I’ll give an example of what a loaded call looks like out of the local 1245 California. The call will say 5-8s single sub ($50 a day) backyard climbing no access poison oak, tankers endorsement and many other things. This could be a loaded call. When a company is looking for a certain person off the books they will put calls in like this deter people from taking the call. Notice I said could be the case, there is a slim chance that the call is that bad. No one travels to California to work 40 hours a week. So, taking one of these calls you’ll probably get spun.

sections.title: Getting Spun
content: When you take a call get a referral and call your GF. He may “spin you.” This is where the company is looking for someone specific or you don’t have the experience requested on the call. For example, the call says need underground splicing experience. You may not have enough or any at all. You’ve been spun; this means that you’ll be put back on the books in the position you were in when you took the call. With the same number of strikes. Getting spun does not count as a strike. The company may pay $50 to you in the form of a gift card. I know this is the case out of local 1245. The rules are different across jurisdictions. Call the hall for better details. If the same call gets to you the next day and you take it again, you’ll likely get spun again.

sections.title: Waiting For The Call
content: I'll keep this section brief and expand on details in later parts. Once you’ve signed up and you know the rules of the locals. You know how the strike process works. You’re waiting for the hall to call you with jobs. Depending on the local, you may have to bid on the jobs. Either through the local’s website or by calling and requesting a job. For example, the local 1245 California will call you with jobs available to you. They call this time “Dispatch” typically starts at 9:00am. Check with the hall on when to call and ask questions and signing the books. You don’t want to try to sign the books during dispatch. In this example we will use the local 1249 in New York. You must bid on the job to be eligible for the call.  If you do not bid on calls you will not get the calls. This is why it’s important to know how the local dispatches calls. If there are 100 hands on book 2 and 10 of the book 2 hands bid on the same job Dispatch will figure out where the 10 hands are on book 2 and call the highest hand that bid the call. By this time, you’ve had time to think about where you want to work, and the type of work. Well talk about where you will be staying in a later section.

sections.title: You Got The Call
content: Congratulations, you got your first call. Now the fun begins. Only a few more technical things to learn before we get into the other things. you get referral, verify all the information on the referral is correct, you speak with your GF, he doesn’t spin you. He gives you the information about on-boarding. Now let’s remember that you signed multiple books. Now is the time that you need to call every hall that you signed and have them remove you from their books. This ensures that you aren’t “Double Booking”.
checklist: Verify referral details (hours, per diem/sub, address, show-up time)
Call the GF ASAP with any questions
Remove yourself from all other books to avoid double booking

sections.title: Double Booking
content: Where a person is currently working while still signed up on the work out workbooks. This is a huge problem. If you think about it, you’re working and holding on to a spot on other books that another hand could have. Preventing him from getting a job sooner while he is out of work. This is completely against what the union stands for. This is a brotherhood, where we help each other. Don’t double book. There are huge consequences associated with it. When you get caught, you will have to stand before the E-board and explain yourself. Good luck because it’s an unexplainable act. Your ticket could be stripped of you. They will black ball you from working on their property. To name a few. This includes short calls, storm calls, and working non-union craft positions which we will discuss in more detail later.

sections.title: Finding A Place To Stay
content: You took your call. Hopefully it’s where you want to work in the desired state, you’re in. You’ve had time to research the area for a place to stay. You may have to slum it for a few days in a hotel until you figure it out. I’ll explain a few options that I prefer to use.
checklist: Choose housing strategy (Furnished Finder, Airbnb, camper, hotel)
Research the area before you show up
Have a backup plan for the first few nights

sections.title: Furnished Finder
content: An app designed for traveling nurses. Fully furnished homes or rooms in homes that have a month-to-month lease. This is my preferred way to find a place to stay. You can create an account for free and send a housing request in the desired area. Once you do this people will send you, their listings. You can set up walk throughs, talk to the landlords, read reviews of the homes. It’s simple, the houses will typically have starter toiletry items, trash bags, dish soap, and many more. This is nice so you don’t have to travel so heavy with unnecessary things. This tends to be less expensive in comparison to staying in a hotel, and you aren’t so restricted. It is nice if you’re traveling in a group. You can all split the rent and have a nice place to stay. Things to consider, if you’re show up is in a remote area you could run the risk of finding a place. In my experience I haven’t ever had a problem finding a place. You must grind to find a place quickly. Don’t be afraid to call the landlords. One caution, be aware that if you end up dragging your job, getting laid off, or worst case fired you will have trouble breaking the lease. Some landlords will work with you some wont. Be sure to negotiate.
checklist: Create an account and submit a housing request
Call landlords and schedule walkthroughs
Negotiate flexibility in case of layoff/dragging

sections.title: Air B&B
content: I think this is self-explanatory. This choice is most of the time more expensive. The availability is spotty since most will allow for short weekend vacations where furnished finder doesn’t. Having the potential for you to have to move out when the landlords have other tenants coming in for the weekend. Inconvenient, but doable if the deal is good enough and it’s close to the show up. Although you can find good deals you just have to hustle a little harder, but it’s possible. Same cautions as above.

sections.title: Camper
content: This choice is favored by many. It can be the cheapest choice depending on the situation. If you currently own a camper and a truck to pull it. It would probably be a great choice. In my opinion I don’t think buying a camper and a truck to pull it is the best choice. That is a big investment in something that may not be for you. Totally my opinion. If you go this route here are some things to consider. Are there going to be campgrounds within a driving distance that you’re comfortable driving. If you’ve never lived in a camper full time it comes with its own set of challenges. You own it you fix it. Some people love this option some people hate it. The campgrounds are awesome for a family environment. There will be many families just like yours in the campground. This can help ease some of the anxiety of having to meet new people in a new place. Also helps with networking, which is a critical part of being on the outside. Same cautions as above. Consider your goals, what’s your plan with the camper when you’re done traveling? Do you own a home or is your camper your home?
checklist: Confirm campgrounds within a reasonable commute
Plan for maintenance and utilities
Decide what you’ll do with the camper when traveling ends

sections.title: Networking
content: Now you have had time to prove yourself to the guys with which you are working. You start building your network. Its easy, be a good person. Show up on time ready to work. Do your best to retain the new spec. Pull your weight on the crew. You will be able to tell if you are pulling your weight. People are quick to tell you if you are not. Once people see that you are a worker “hand” they will tell other people about you. That is where the fire starts, it’s up to you to keep your name in good standing. Your name is everything, it will follow you wherever you go. Keep the dirt off your name, it’s not hard. You also just need to talk to your brothers that you work with. Brothers at the campground. Be careful who you consider having in your network. Birds of a feather flock together.
checklist: Show up on time and pull your weight
Build relationships with brothers on the crew and campground
Protect your reputation—your name travels

sections.title: Lets Drag
content: At this point you have been working. Hopefully enjoy your new job. Learning new things. There will come a time when you have had enough or want something different. Or you have made a network and heard that there is better money somewhere else. So, you decide to drag. This means to quit. You can decide how you would like to do it. If the company has treated, you poorly and you feel it necessary to leave them in a bind you quit on the spot. Or if you want to give a heads up you can do so. Things to consider, you want to have something lined up. This does not mean double booking. Dragging a job without something lined up can be good or bad. If work is moving well enough that you will not have a problem getting a job within a week, no big deal. If work is slow you need to use your network to find out where to go before just dragging up. Dragging will cost you money. Think about it, you could have to find a new place to stay, potentially have to travel out of the current state you are working in. You may not get a job as soon as you want depending on work. Just something to consider.
checklist: Use your network to find the next move
Budget for travel and temporary housing between jobs
Avoid double booking while lining up the next job

sections.title: Term Slip
content: Short for termination slip is a form saying you willingly quit, got layoff, or fired. Once you obtain the slip you will need it at most locals to get back on the books. If you’re signing for the first time they won’t, ask you for a term slip.
checklist: Get a term slip when you quit/are laid off/terminated
Keep it for book placement at locals that require it

sections.title: Layoffs
content: They are real, and they suck, but it is a part of the game. Reduction in force due to lack of work. You will hear the comment of a “one-man layoff” what this mean is that one guy isn’t fitting in or isn’t pulling his weight. Instead of firing the guy they will lay him off. This does two things. One it allows that guy to apply for unemployment, where if he were fired, he wouldn’t be able to collect unemployment. Keep this in mind when you drag you willingly quit so you won’t be able to collect unemployment. The second thing is if you get fired for lack of performance the hall will want to E-board you. You do not want to be in that situation. They can decide that you’re not fit to work on the property and black ball you from the hall.

sections.title: Two Checked
content: Common terminology for getting laid off or fired “They just two check bobby”. If more than one guy is getting laid off the word gets around the show up quick. Usually with enough time to figure out what you are going to do. This is a good reason to stay active with your network. Keep feelers out at all times, you never know. In my experience I never got suddenly laid off. But I did get told that we had a ton of work after a job that we were currently on and toward the end of the current job it all changed. That is the closest I’ve been to a surprise layoff. You might hear a guy “give me my term slip and my two checks” all this means is he’s dragging and going back to the hall to sign the books. The two checks part of that comment refers to getting your last two checks from your employer. Example if you drag on pay day you will only need to get one check. That will be the money that you earned for the week after the check you get on pay day. If you drag the Monday before pay day you will get two checks the check you were due that pay day for the previous week and the check for everything after that previous week. Depending on the locals rules, the company must give you those two checks that day. If not, the company will be fined and own you money. As I said this is based on the locals contract.
